name: Danuglipron

lead: Danuglipron is an investigational, non-peptide pill that activates the GLP-1 receptor, the target of semaglutide and tirzepatide. It was studied for type 2 diabetes and obesity.

The appearance link is weight and body-fat reduction. Meta-analyses of randomized trials report lower weight and blood sugar than control, but Wikipedia reports Pfizer ended development in April 2025 because of hard-to-predict liver toxicity, so it is not available as a medicine.

paras: It was taken by mouth in trials, in immediate-release (twice daily) and modified-release forms. Because it was never approved, there is no standard use; it appears in discussion as an oral alternative to GLP-1 injections.
Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were the most reported effects in trials; development ended because of liver toxicity. It has no approval and should be regarded as unavailable outside trials.

angle.text: Like other GLP-1 drugs, danuglipron reduces appetite and weight, which can change body composition and facial leanness. It was investigational only and is no longer in development.

lead: Danuglipron (PF-06882961) is an experimental oral small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist developed by Pfizer for type 2 diabetes and obesity.[1] Unlike peptide drugs such as semaglutide, it is a non-peptide that can be swallowed.[2]

Randomized trials in type 2 diabetes and obesity reported greater reductions in HbA1c and body weight than control.[3][4] A 2025 meta-analysis of eight studies found danuglipron reduced weight by about 2.2 kg on average versus baseline comparisons.[4]
In April 2025 Pfizer announced it would end development because of liver toxicity that was difficult to predict.[1]

paras: Danuglipron binds the GLP-1 receptor, raising insulin in a glucose-dependent way, slowing gastric emptying and increasing satiety, according to a reference summary.[5] It was developed as immediate-release and modified-release oral formulations.[5]

A meta-analysis of seven randomized trials of orforglipron and danuglipron, with 1,037 patients, found significant reductions in HbA1c and weight versus controls.[3] A later meta-analysis of eight studies reported danuglipron lowered HbA1c, fasting glucose and weight.[4] A 2026 review places it among oral GLP-1 agents alongside injectables like semaglutide and tirzepatide.[2]
Wikipedia reports nausea, diarrhea and vomiting were the most common side effects and that Pfizer stopped development in April 2025 over liver toxicity.[1]

timeline.event: Pfizer announces end of danuglipron development (April).[1]
